Building the roadmap around one high-profile client Ignoring the economic buyer’s success criteria Delaying integrations Targeting too many segments before the core use case is proven Building for the User and the Buyer Product Management Startup B2B SaaS Product Strategy How to Build a B2B Product Strategy When the User Isn’t the Buyer The UX Design Stack 11 min read · Oct 21, 2026 -- Listen Share Selling to businesses and selling to consumers share one thing: you need a product people want. Beyond that, the rules are different. B2B purchases involve multiple stakeholders, longer timelines, compliance requirements, and integration dependencies that most consumer-facing companies never encounter. A solid B2B product strategy accounts for all of it, from the product experience itself to the entire path from first conversation to signed contract. In B2B, the person using your product and the person paying for it are usually two different people, and your strategy has to win over both. That starts with a precise customer profile and problem validation across the whole buying committee, then carries through a vision tied to business outcomes and a roadmap that clears deal blockers early. Priorities and metrics change as the company grows, and four specific mistakes can sink a product that’s technically solid. Press enter or click to view image in full size Why Does B2B Product Strategy Differ From B2C? B2B product strategy operates under a set of structural constraints that most consumer product frameworks don’t account for. The most immediate one is the buying committee . A consumer makes a purchase decision alone. In B2B, the same decision typically involves the end user, their manager, IT, legal, and procurement, each evaluating the product through a completely different lens. A product can solve the user’s problem and still get blocked by a security review or stall because the budget owner was never brought into the conversation. Decision maker. In B2C, one person decides. In B2B, several stakeholders do. Sales cycle. Consumer purchases close in hours or days. B2B deals take weeks at minimum, and enterprise contracts can stretch past a year. Integrations. For consumers, they’re a nice extra. Many businesses won’t sign without them. Compliance. It rarely comes up in a consumer purchase. In B2B, it frequently gates the deal. User = buyer? In B2C, usually yes. In B2B, often no. Two of these deserve extra attention for product teams. Integrations and compliance count as purchasing prerequisites for many organizations. A product that doesn’t connect to an existing CRM or hasn’t completed a SOC 2 audit will lose deals regardless of how well it performs. The user-buyer gap shapes every prioritization decision. The person who will use the product daily rarely signs the contract. The person who signs the contract may never open the app. B2B product strategy has to account for both: what earns user enthusiasm and what earns buyer confidence. Step 1: Who Is Your Ideal Customer? Your B2B ideal customer profile (ICP) is the starting point for every other strategic decision. Get it wrong, and the roadmap, the messaging, and the go-to-market motion all point in the wrong direction. Most early-stage teams define their ICP too broadly, with labels like “mid-market SaaS companies” or “healthcare organizations.” That level of description leaves too many open questions to act on. A useful ICP answers three things with precision. 1. Who the company is Industry, company size, revenue range, and existing tech stack The specific use case that makes your product relevant to them right now Signs that the problem is urgent enough to justify a purchase decision 2. Who inside the company you are dealing with B2B purchases involve more than one person, and each role has different concerns. Mapping the buying committee is a separate exercise from defining your user persona. End user. Their question is the most personal one: does this make my daily work easier? Manager or champion. They want to know if it solves the team’s problem and if they can confidently advocate for it. IT and security. Their review checks compliance and integration requirements. Economic buyer. They look at ROI and how the purchase fits the budget. 3. How fit customers differ from low-fit ones A high-fit customer experiences the problem your product solves as an active priority, has the budget authority to act, and operates in a context where your product runs without heavy customization.
